claims.text: Thermal processing can control local chemical ordering and defect distributions in multiprincipal-element alloys.
Increasing local chemical ordering and modifying defect distributions promotes formation of a stable, adherent oxide scale.
The resulting oxide scale impedes oxygen transport.
The proposed thermal-processing-induced state retains mechanical integrity under high-temperature oxidizing conditions.
Equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn is an example of the multiprincipal-element alloy system considered.
The initial alloy is homogenized and solutionized with minimal compositional gradients.
Varying solutionizing temperature and cooling rate can tailor short-range order and defect density without changing nominal composition.
The controlled test uses long-duration oxidation-fatigue exposure in air at 1000–1100 °C for at least approximately 100 hours.
Local chemical ordering and defect clusters at grain boundaries or within grains influence oxide-scale adherence.
Local chemical ordering and defect clusters influence mechanical stress distribution.
Specific short-range order reduces metal-cation and oxygen diffusion through the developing oxide.
Reduced diffusion through the oxide produces a more protective scale.
The ordered microstructure distributes mechanical load more uniformly and thereby improves mechanical robustness.
A higher degree of short-range order will produce slower oxide-growth kinetics than a lower-order reference state.
A higher degree of short-range order will improve high-temperature mechanical performance relative to a lower-order reference state.
Rapid quenching from a higher solutionizing temperature minimizes short-range order and can provide the lower-order baseline.
The hypothesis applies primarily to single- or dual-phase, near-equiatomic multiprincipal-element alloys whose phase constitution is stable at or above 900 °C.
At higher temperatures or in complex multiphase materials, additional diffusion pathways may dominate and limit the ordering effect.
Grain size and secondary phases may confound the inferred contribution of short-range order.
Failure of changes in short-range order to significantly affect both oxidation rate and high-temperature mechanical stability relative to the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.
